title: India Bank Deposits Hit Record $3 Trillion After Dollar Scheme Surge
excerpt: RBI data show deposits at about 284 trillion rupees in late September after a discounted dollar swap window drew roughly $133 billion before closing a month early.
body:
• Indian banking system deposits reached about 284 trillion rupees ($2.99 trillion) in the second half of September, Reserve Bank of India data cited by Reuters show.
  • Deposits rose 21.67 trillion rupees in the first half of the financial year, including about 20 trillion rupees between June 16 and August 31 while a discounted dollar swap window was open.
  • The scheme drew about $133 billion and closed on August 31, a month early; the foreign-currency window is now closed, so new NRI dollar deposits under those terms are no longer available.
  • CareEdge Ratings expects term deposit rates to face upward pressure after an October rate hike, as credit grows faster than deposits and the liquidity surplus shrinks — savers comparing fixed deposits should check rates again before locking in.

India's banking system deposits rose to a record of around 284 trillion rupees, or $2.99 trillion, in the second half of September, according to central bank data reported by Reuters. The increase was driven in large part by a temporary Reserve Bank of India facility designed to pull dollar deposits into the banking system.

How the record was built

Deposits increased by 21.67 trillion rupees in the first six months of the financial year, taking the September-end total 8.4% above the March-end level. About 20 trillion rupees of that rise came between June 16 and August 31, the period when the RBI's discounted swap window was operating.

The RBI announced the window in June to attract foreign-currency deposits and encouraged lenders to raise cheaper funding. Banks raised dollar deposits, including foreign-currency non-resident deposits, and swapped the dollars with the central bank at a discounted rate, converting them into rupee liquidity. Inflows reached about $133 billion, and the RBI closed the window on August 31, a month earlier than planned.

A second, routine factor added to the total at quarter-end. Lenders built funding buffers before September 30, and deposits rose by 7.73 trillion rupees in the fortnight ending that date.

Expensive money, thinner margins

The inflow solved a funding problem that had built up over several years, when credit grew faster than deposits and banks relied more on market borrowing and costly bulk deposits. Analysis by Upstox, citing RBI data, notes the new dollar money is locked in for three to five years but costs banks about 6.65% once interest and hedging on the interest portion are included — above the 5.90% average cost of fresh rupee fixed deposits in July.

That cost matters because banks must lend the money at a margin. Parking it with the central bank earns less than it costs, government bonds barely cover it, and fresh lending earns less than the existing loan book on average, rating agency analysis cited in that coverage noted. Banks with strong retail lending franchises can deploy the funds more patiently; banks that raised dollars mainly to fill a funding gap face more pressure.

What it means for savers and borrowers

While the system was in surplus, competition for deposits stayed contained, CareEdge Ratings said. That is unlikely to persist if loan demand continues to outpace deposit growth. CareEdge said an October rate hike rules out further cuts in term deposit rates for now and is likely to push them up as the surplus shrinks, a view also summarised by Finimize.

For NRI savers, the specific opportunity has passed: the discounted swap-backed scheme closed early after reaching about $133 billion, so the rates offered under it cannot be assumed for new deposits. For savers in India, the practical implication is the opposite direction — fixed deposit rates are more likely to rise than fall in the near term, making it worth comparing tenures before committing long-term funds.

What to watch

September-quarter bank results will show how quickly lenders are deploying the new deposits and what the funding cost does to net interest margins. The other variables are credit growth, festive-season cash demand and how fast the liquidity surplus normalises now that the one-off inflow has ended. The record headline is a stock figure; the test is whether deposit growth stays close to credit growth without the swap window.
